title: Learning Paths for All 36 Weekly Problems
summary: Master Learning Paths for All 36 Weekly Problems through explanation, prediction, implementation, and review.

challenges.title: Recall checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Without reopening the lesson, explain Learning Paths for All 36 Weekly Problems in your own words. Include the problem it solves, the core mechanism, and one boundary or failure.
challenges.hint: Use “Week 1: Repository contract” as a cue, then close the lesson again.

challenges.title: Prediction checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Choose one example or source file from this mission. Predict its behavior for a normal input and a changed or invalid input before running or revealing the reference. Explain the rule separating the outcomes.
challenges.hint: Change one condition at a time so the result teaches a rule.

challenges.title: Build and prove checkpoint
challenges.prompt: Implement, debug, or adapt the mission exercise yourself. Record the acceptance criterion, command or interaction used to verify it, failure evidence, and one tradeoff. Do not paste the reference solution.
challenges.hint: A passing check, measured result, focused diff, or reproducible demo is stronger than ‘done.’

files.content:
# Learning Paths for All 36 Weekly Problems

Use this alongside [the practice problems](CURRICULUM-PRACTICE.md). Each row
offers an effective entry mode, a concrete artifact, and a second mode that
forces transfer. The entry is a suggestion, not a label: choose another mode
from [LEARNING-MODES.md](LEARNING-MODES.md) if your lowest score is elsewhere.

Before every problem, predict an outcome without notes. After every problem,
preserve evidence, explain one tradeoff, and schedule a delayed retry.

## Week 1: Repository contract

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Cold-clone rehearsal | Map-first: diagram every prerequisite and startup boundary, then annotate where the README supplied it. | Written synthesis: rewrite ambiguous setup steps for a stranger and repeat from a clean environment. |
| Three intentional CI failures | Test-first: predict which stage and message each defect triggers before pushing it. | Teach-back: explain what each gate proves and, importantly, what it does not prove. |
| Decision under constraints | Rule-first: list constraints and decision criteria before comparing tools. | Collaborative review: have someone argue for the rejected option and record what would reverse the decision. |

## Week 2: Testing strategy

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Put each risk at the cheapest boundary | Map-first: place risks on a unit/component/integration/browser test pyramid. | Example-first: implement one representative check at two levels and compare speed, fidelity, and diagnosis. |
| Expose an order-dependent test | Example-first: trace shared state across two execution orders. | Error-driven: record the false assumption, isolate state, and rerun in shuffled or repeated order. |
| Regression-first repair | Test-first: reproduce the defect with the smallest failing test before changing code. | Teach-back: explain why the test belongs at that layer and which nearby bug remains uncovered. |

## Week 3: Relational data

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Make invalid state impossible in SQL | Rule-first: write each domain invariant and its database enforcement point. | Example-first: attempt valid and invalid inserts, then explain which layer rejected each case. |
| Index from a query | Map-first: mark filter, join, sort, and returned columns in a query-flow sketch. | Test-first: capture query plans before and after the index with representative data. |
| Expand and contract | Map-first: draw old/new application versions across each migration phase. | Collaborative review: let a reviewer search for a deployment order that breaks compatibility. |

## Week 4: HTTP API contract

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate creation | Example-first: timeline the original request, lost response, and retry. | Test-first: prove one durable change under sequential and concurrent duplicate requests. |
| Change data between pages | Map-first: draw the cursor position before and after an insertion or deletion. | Rule-first: state the total-order predicate and construct a tied-value counterexample. |
| Contract mismatch | Rule-first: compare the OpenAPI contract with observed success and error responses. | Test-first: create a contract check that fails for the mismatch, then repair the responsible side. |

## Week 5: Production React

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Enumerate every async screen | Map-first: build a UI state machine for idle, loading, empty, success, stale, and error. | Test-first: trigger every transition and assert user-visible behavior. |
| Keyboard-only journey | Build-first: complete the journey without a pointer and record every block. | Collaborative review: have another person repeat it while narrating focus and expected controls. |
| Measure before memoizing | Rule-first: predict the expensive render and define a meaningful measurement. | Error-driven: profile, change one cause, remeasure, and record whether the prediction was wrong. |

## Week 6: Authentication and authorization

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| ID substitution matrix | Example-first: vary actor, board, card, and membership while predicting every result. | Test-first: automate the forbidden combinations and verify responses do not leak resource existence. |
| Session lifecycle | Map-first: draw issue, use, expiration, revocation, and theft paths. | Teach-back: narrate both a normal sign-out and a compromised-session response. |
| Threat-to-test traceability | Rule-first: connect each asset and threat to a mitigation and observable check. | Collaborative review: let a reviewer invent an abuse case not covered by the matrix. |

## Week 7: Reliability

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicate delivery | Example-first: trace two deliveries through claim, side effect, completion, and retry states. | Test-first: force concurrency and prove the chosen delivery guarantee. |
| Bounded overload | Map-first: sketch queue capacity, admission, processing, rejection, and recovery. | Rule-first: define overload invariants, then load-test the boundary rather than only the happy path. |
| Graceful shutdown | Test-first: terminate during active work and observe what is lost or duplicated. | Teach-back: explain the shutdown order, time bound, and behavior after the deadline. |

## Week 8: Observability

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Request-ID investigation | Map-first: trace one identifier across service and data boundaries. | Collaborative review: give only the identifier to a partner and observe whether the evidence is sufficient. |
| Seeded-secret audit | Error-driven: seed a known fake secret and search every log/output sink. | Rule-first: write a redaction policy, its enforcement locations, and its unavoidable limits. |
| Health semantics | Rule-first: define liveness, readiness, and dependency health separately. | Test-first: fail dependencies one at a time and assert orchestration-relevant responses. |

## Week 9: Delivery

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Reproducible artifact | Test-first: build twice from the documented inputs and compare identified outputs. | Written synthesis: document versions, provenance, and any source of nondeterminism. |
| Migration-order rehearsal | Map-first: create a timeline for old/new code and old/new schema combinations. | Collaborative review: have an operator choose an unexpected rollout or rollback point. |
| Recovery exercise | Teach-back: narrate the runbook before using it, including stop conditions. | Error-driven: run the exercise, record every missing assumption, and revise the runbook from evidence. |

## Week 10: Debugging and maintenance

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Hypothesis ledger | Written synthesis: rank hypotheses with predicted observations before investigating. | Test-first: run the cheapest discriminating experiment and update confidence without rewriting history. |
| Profile a realistic bottleneck | Example-first: choose representative data and predict the hot path. | Error-driven: measure, optimize one cause, and explain any disagreement between intuition and profile. |
| Backward-compatible rename | Map-first: locate every producer, consumer, stored value, and deployment version. | Test-first: prove mixed-version compatibility through expansion, transition, and cleanup. |

## Week 11: System design

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Unit-bearing estimates | Rule-first: write inputs with units and show dimensional calculations. | Verbal rehearsal: explain which assumption dominates and how measurement would update it. |
| Hot-board failure | Map-first: identify contention, fan-out, storage, cache, and connection bottlenecks. | Example-first: walk a single popular board through normal load and 10× load, then propose a measured experiment. |
| Simplest evolution | Written synthesis: compare the current system, one incremental change, and premature redesign. | Collaborative review: defend the simplest change against failure and growth counterexamples. |

## Week 12: Portfolio and interviews

| Problem | Suggested entry and artifact | Rotate to prove transfer |
|---|---|---|
| Five-minute stranger test | Collaborative review: observe a new person use the repository without rescuing them. | Written synthesis: turn every confusion into a specific repository or documentation change. |
| Three-depth explanation | Teach-back: prepare 30-second, 2-minute, and 5-minute versions from five keywords. | Example-first: anchor each version to a demo, failure, measurement, or test. |
| Claim audit | Rule-first: label every portfolio claim as demonstrated, measured, reviewed, or assumed. | Test-first: reproduce each important claim and remove or qualify anything that lacks evidence. |

## Alternative mode substitutions

If the suggested entry does not address your current gap:

- replace map-first with a text sequence or state table when diagrams create a
  barrier;
- replace solo teach-back with a recording when no partner is available;
- replace live collaboration with an overnight self-review or asynchronous
  diff review;
- replace a long build block with three short sessions, but preserve the final
  executable check;
- begin from a worked input when blank-page load is high, then change the input
  and reconstruct the rule without the example;
- add a concept map when code details obscure system boundaries;
- add an error ledger when repeated fixes are not changing future predictions.

## Completion rule

A checked box in the practice file means the task was attempted. Mastery means
you can repeat the essential reasoning after a delay, handle a changed case,
and explain the evidence. Track those separately in [PROGRESS.md](PROGRESS.md).
